A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OT-CP research. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, regression evaluations on six real datasets, and classification results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, including appendix experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original regression and classification experiments, supplemented by runtime measurements and additional classification scenarios in Appendix D.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces v1's fixed rank threshold with split calibration: D1 learns the transport map and D2 calibrates its threshold. OT-CP+ likewise replaces its fixed neighborhood-based threshold with a threshold calibrated across held-out conditional ranks. These change both procedures, rather than merely documenting them.

E1.justification: v2 removes the five-class CIFAR-10 evaluation, eliminating the natural-image benchmark, and adds five-class MNIST and a synthetic classification scenario with less-confusable classes. The six regression datasets and full MNIST/Fashion-MNIST tasks remain. Thus represented image domains and classification scenarios change substantially.

E2.justification: Predictive baseline membership remains ELL/REC for synthetic regression, adaptive ELL for real regression, and IP/MS/APS for classification. Figure 12 newly compares OT-CP and OT-CP+ runtimes, adding a limited comparison between existing variants. Newly cited competing approaches are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: MNIST/Fashion-MNIST experiments change from 20,000 observations with a 10%/80%/10% train/calibration/test split to 25,000 with 10%/45%/45%. Calibration now includes D1/D2 splitting. Appendix D.2 additionally reports a square-root neighborhood rule for larger datasets, while new experiments vary calibration size and measure runtime, marginal coverage, and volume.

E4.justification: Appendix D.4 adds runtime scaling with calibration size and a controlled comparison of more versus less-confusable synthetic classes. These investigate computational scalability and when classification advantages arise, extending v1's existing five-versus-ten-class analysis. Figure 13 also exposes coverage, volume, and runtime tradeoffs in real regression.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten repeated random draws for the image-classification experiments and display error bars. v2 does not introduce a changed repetition policy, seed specification, confidence-interval definition, or significance-testing procedure. Changed error-bar magnitudes are result changes.

E6.justification: Numerous plotted results change. For example, Figure 4's low-data wq worst-set coverage for the adaptive method falls from approximately 0.92 to 0.79. New runtime, regression-efficiency, easier-classification, and five-class MNIST results appear, while CIFAR-10 results disappear. Given the method and protocol revisions, these are replaced or newly reported outcomes, not controlled same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.4 changes its upper bound from alpha + 2/(n+1) to alpha + n_ties/(n2+1), with rewritten exchangeability arguments and a generalized tie lemma. Theorem 3.2 now specifies convergence in probability as both calibration subsets grow. Appendix B adds threshold-consistency Lemma B.2 and substantially replaces the conditional-coverage proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain multivariate OT-based prediction regions, finite-sample marginal coverage, and asymptotic conditional coverage. The conclusion now explicitly qualifies the efficiency advantages by acknowledging potentially more conservative regression sets and greater computational cost, modestly narrowing the overall contribution narrative.

C2.justification: v2 explains why distribution-free fitted ranks alone do not justify the original coverage argument and motivates separate calibration. It adds substantive limitations concerning small-sample overcoverage, set-size and runtime costs, and opportunities for alternative reference distributions or entropic maps. Appendix D.4 also interprets classification benefits through label-confusion patterns.

D1.justification: Appendix D.1 newly identifies the network simplex solver in Python Optimal Transport; this is a disclosure, not evidence of a solver change. v2 adds neighborhood-size guidance and specifies the five-class MNIST labels. The CIFAR-10 neural-network architecture details disappear with that experiment.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning across copula, multiple-testing, latent-space, density/sampling, and shape-optimization approaches. v2 discusses concurrent work by Klein, Dheur, Braun, and Luo and Zhou, including the relationship between OT-CP and entropic transport-based conformal prediction.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 expands procedural explanations, reorganizes the appendices into methodology, proofs, related work, and experiments, and adds an Impact Statement and affiliation edits. Much of the substantial rewriting accompanies scientific changes rather than an independent overhaul of the narrative.

P2.justification: Classification displays are reorganized into aggregated main-text metrics and paired label-wise coverage plots, with detailed results in the appendix. New runtime, regression-tradeoff, easier-classification, and MNIST-subset figures appear; CIFAR-10's figure disappears. Existing figures also receive layout, caption, and legend revisions, including identifying OT-CP+ correctly in Figure 4.

improvement.justification: The separate map-fitting and threshold-calibration stages address the exchangeability gap underlying v1's central coverage argument, substantially improving the paper's theoretical foundation. Added computational evidence, implementation details, and explicit limitations improve assessability. Removing CIFAR-10 narrows empirical breadth, and Section 3.2 still overstates Figure 4's worst-set coverage, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the repair of the main validity argument and fuller accounting of practical tradeoffs.
